e-13186.knowledge_point: Expressing a Given Set Using an Arithmetic Sequence
e-13186.problem:
Describe the set $S=\{... , -5, -3, -1, 1, 3, ...\}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take $a_1 = 1$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*
e-13186.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
\ldots, \quad -5, \quad -3, \quad -1, \quad 1, \quad 3, \quad \ldots
$$

form a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =2 \\  & =-3-(-5) \\  & =-1-(-3) \\  & =1-(-1) \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  $a_1=1,$ the $n$th term $a_n$ of our sequence for $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)\cdot d \\  & =1+(n-1)\cdot 2 \\  & =1+2n-2 \\  & =2n-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S = \big\{2n-1 \: : \: n \in \mathbb{Z}\big\}
$$

**Watch Out!** 

The constructive definition of a set is typically not unique. 

Since the elements of $A$ are generated by a *two-way* infinite arithmetic sequence, we could have picked *any* term in our sequence as $a_1$ when determining $a_n.$ We selected $a_1 = 1$ because this led to a nice, simple expression in our constructive definition.

e-13184.knowledge_point: Expressing a Given Set Using a Geometric Sequence
e-13184.problem:
Describe the set $S=\left\{\ldots, -36, -6, -1, -\dfrac1{6}, -\dfrac1{36}, ...\right\}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take $a_1 = -\dfrac16$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*
e-13184.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
\ldots,\quad -36, \quad -6, \quad -1, \quad -\dfrac1{6}, \quad -\dfrac1{36}, \quad \ldots
$$

form a two-way infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=\dfrac16{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\frac{1}{6} \\  & =(\frac{-6}{-36}) \\  & =(\frac{-1}{-6}) \\  & =\frac{(-\frac{1}{6})}{(-1)} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  $a_1=-\dfrac16,$ the $n$th term $a_n$ of our sequence for $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =(-\frac{1}{6})\cdot {(\frac{1}{6})}^{n-1} \\  & =-(\frac{1}{6})\cdot {(\frac{1}{6})}^{-1}\cdot {(\frac{1}{6})}^{n} \\  & =-{(\frac{1}{6})}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S = \left\{-\left(\dfrac16\right)^{n} \: : \: n\in \mathbb{Z}\right\}
$$

e-13144.knowledge_point: Expressing a Set Using a Conditional Definition
e-13144.problem: Describe the set $S = \{-9,-8,-7, ..., 5\}$ using a conditional definition.
e-13144.worked_solution:
The set $S$ contains all integer numbers between $-9$ and $5$ (including $-9$ and $5$).

Therefore, the set can be written as

$$
S = \{ x \in \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\mathbb Z} \: : \: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}-9} \leq x \leq \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}5} \}.
$$

**Note**: This definition is not unique. For example, we can write $S$ equivalently as follows:

$$
S = \big\{ x \in \mathbb Z \: : \: -10 \lt x \lt 6 \big\}
$$

e-13185.knowledge_point: Defining a Set Conditionally Using the Roots of a Polynomial
e-13185.problem:
Find the missing coefficients $p$ and $q$ in the conditional definition of the set given below.

$$
\{\pm 3\textrm{i}\} = \Big\{z \in \mathbb{C} \: : \: 4z^2+pz+q = 0 \Big\}
$$
e-13185.worked_solution:
The given set contains the roots $z\in\mathbb C$ of some quadratic polynomial $f(z).$

Since the quadratic polynomial has roots $z_1=-3\textrm{i}$ and $z_2=3\textrm{i},$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=4,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(z) & =a(z-{z}_{1})(z-{z}_{2}) \\  & =4\cdot (z-(-3\text{i}))(z-(3\text{i})) \\  & =4\cdot (z+3\text{i})(z-3\text{i}) \\  & =4\cdot ({z}^{2}-(3\text{i})^{2}) \\  & =4\cdot ({z}^{2}-9{\text{i}}^{2}) \\  & =4\cdot ({z}^{2}+9) \\  & =4{z}^{2}+36\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can express the given set as follows:

$$
\{\pm 3\textrm{i}\} = \Big\{z \in \mathbb{C} \: : \: 4z^2+\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0}z+\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}36} = 0 \Big\}
$$

Finally, $p=0$ and $q=36.$

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Describe the set $S={...,-4,-2,0,2,4,...}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=2$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

$$
2n
$$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,-4,\,-2,\,0,\,2,\,4,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =2 \\  & =-2-(-4) \\  & =0-(-2) \\  & =2-0 \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=2,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)\cdot d \\  & =2+(n-1)\cdot 2 \\  & =2+2n-2 \\  & =2n.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={2n\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

Notice that the elements of our set …,−4,−2,0,2,4,… form a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence with common difference d=2:

d=2=−2−(−4)=0−(−2)=2−0=⋯

content.problem:
Describe the set $S={...,-4,-2,0,2,4,...}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=2$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

$$
2n+1
$$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,-4,\,-2,\,0,\,2,\,4,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =2 \\  & =-2-(-4) \\  & =0-(-2) \\  & =2-0 \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=2,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)\cdot d \\  & =2+(n-1)\cdot 2 \\  & =2+2n-2 \\  & =2n.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={2n\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Describe the set $S={...,-21,-17,-13,-9,-5,...}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=-5$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

$$
n+4
$$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,-21,\,-17,\,-13,\,-9,\,-5,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =4 \\  & =-17-(-21) \\  & =-13-(-17) \\  & =-9-(-13) \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=-5,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)\cdot d \\  & =-5+(n-1)\cdot 4 \\  & =-5+4n-4 \\  & =4n-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={4n-9\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Expressing a Given Set Using an Arithmetic Sequence
content.problem:
Describe the set $S={...,-21,-17,-13,-9,-5,...}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=-5$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

$$
4n-9
$$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,-21,\,-17,\,-13,\,-9,\,-5,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =4 \\  & =-17-(-21) \\  & =-13-(-17) \\  & =-9-(-13) \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=-5,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)\cdot d \\  & =-5+(n-1)\cdot 4 \\  & =-5+4n-4 \\  & =4n-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={4n-9\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Describe the set $S={12,9,6,3,...}$ using a constructive definition.

$$
15-3n
$$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
12,\,9,\,6,\,3,\,…
$$

form an arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=-3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =-3 \\  & =9-12 \\  & =6-9 \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in N$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)\cdot d \\  & =12+(n-1)\cdot (-3) \\  & =12-3n+3 \\  & =15-3n.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={15-3n\,:\,n\in N}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Describe the set $S={...,3,6,9,12,15,...}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=3$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

$$
2n-1
$$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,3,\,6,\,9,\,12,\,15,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =3 \\  & =6-3 \\  & =9-6 \\  & =12-9 \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=3,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)\cdot d \\  & =3+(n-1)\cdot 3 \\  & =3+3n-3 \\  & =3n.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={3n\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

EXPLANATION

Notice that the elements of our set …,3,6,9,12,15,… form a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence with common difference d=3:

d=3=6−3=9−6=12−9=⋯

Therefore, setting a1=3, the nth term an of our sequence for n∈Z is given by

an=a1+(n−1)⋅d=3+(n−1)⋅3=3+3n−3=3n.

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

S={3n:n∈Z}

content.problem:
Describe the set $S={...,3,6,9,12,15,...}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=3$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

$$
n+2
$$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,3,\,6,\,9,\,12,\,15,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =3 \\  & =6-3 \\  & =9-6 \\  & =12-9 \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=3,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)\cdot d \\  & =3+(n-1)\cdot 3 \\  & =3+3n-3 \\  & =3n.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={3n\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Describe the set $S={...,-24,-19,-14,-9,-4,...}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=-4$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

$$
5n-9
$$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,-24,\,-19,\,-14,\,-9,\,-4,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =5 \\  & =-19-(-24) \\  & =-14-(-19) \\  & =-9-(-14) \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=-4,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)\cdot d \\  & =-4+(n-1)\cdot 5 \\  & =-4+5n-5 \\  & =5n-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={5n-9\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

Notice that the elements of our set …,−24,−19,−14,−9,−4,… form a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence with common difference d=5:

d=5=−19−(−24)=−14−(−19)=−9−(−14)=⋯

an=a1+(n−1)⋅d=−4+(n−1)⋅5=−4+5n−5=5n−9.

content.problem:
Describe the set $S={...,-24,-19,-14,-9,-4,...}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=-4$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

content.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,-24,\,-19,\,-14,\,-9,\,-4,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =5 \\  & =-19-(-24) \\  & =-14-(-19) \\  & =-9-(-14) \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=-4,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)\cdot d \\  & =-4+(n-1)\cdot 5 \\  & =-4+5n-5 \\  & =5n-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={5n-9\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

$$
\frac{2}{3}\cdot {3}^{n}

after.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
2,\,6,\,18,\,54,\,…
$$

form an infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =3 \\  & =\frac{6}{2} \\  & =\frac{18}{6} \\  & =\frac{54}{18} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in N,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {3}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {3}^{n}\cdot {3}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot {3}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={\frac{2}{3}\cdot {3}^{n}\,:\,n\in N}
$$

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Describe the set $S={…,-2,4,-8,16,-32,...}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=-2$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

$$
{(\frac{1}{2})}^{n}
$$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,-2,\,4,\,-8,\,16,\,-32,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =-2 \\  & =(\frac{4}{-2}) \\  & =(\frac{-8}{4}) \\  & =(\frac{16}{-8}) \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=-2,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =-2\cdot (-2)^{n-1} \\  & =-2\cdot (-2)^{n}\cdot (-2)^{-1} \\  & =\frac{-2}{-2}\cdot (-2)^{n} \\  & =(-2)^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={(-2)^{n}\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

EXPLANATION

Notice that the elements of our set …,−2,4,−8,16,−32,… form a two-way infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio r=−2:

r=−2=(4−2)=(−84)=(16−8)=⋯

Therefore, setting a1=−2, the nth term an of our sequence for n∈Z is given by

an=a1⋅rn−1=−2⋅(−2)n−1=−2⋅(−2)n⋅(−2)−1=−2−2⋅(−2)n=(−2)n.

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

S={(−2)n:n∈Z}

content.knowledge_point: Expressing a Given Set Using a Geometric Sequence
content.problem:
Describe the set $S={…,-2,4,-8,16,-32,...}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=-2$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

$$
(-2)^{n}
$$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,-2,\,4,\,-8,\,16,\,-32,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =-2 \\  & =(\frac{4}{-2}) \\  & =(\frac{-8}{4}) \\  & =(\frac{16}{-8}) \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=-2,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =-2\cdot (-2)^{n-1} \\  & =-2\cdot (-2)^{n}\cdot (-2)^{-1} \\  & =\frac{-2}{-2}\cdot (-2)^{n} \\  & =(-2)^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={(-2)^{n}\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

\begin{aligned}r & =6 \\  & =\frac{24}{4} \\  & =\frac{144}{24} \\  & =\frac{864}{144} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in N,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =4\cdot {6}^{n-1} \\  & =4\cdot {6}^{n}\cdot {6}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot {6}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={\frac{2}{3}\cdot {6}^{n}\,:\,n\in N}
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Describe the set $S={…,3,6,12,24,48,...}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=6$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

$$
\frac{1}{3}\cdot {2}^{n}
$$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,3,\,6,\,12,\,24,\,48,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =2 \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =\frac{12}{6} \\  & =\frac{24}{12} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=6,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =6\cdot {2}^{n-1} \\  & =6\cdot {2}^{n}\cdot {2}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{6}{2}\cdot {2}^{n} \\  & =3\cdot {2}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={3\cdot {2}^{n}\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

EXPLANATION

Notice that the elements of our set …,3,6,12,24,48,… form a two-way infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio r=2:

r=2=63=126=2412=⋯

Therefore, setting a1=6, the nth term an of our sequence for n∈Z is given by

an=a1⋅rn−1=6⋅2n−1=6⋅2n⋅2−1=62⋅2n=3⋅2n

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

S={3⋅2n:n∈Z}

content.problem:
Describe the set $S={…,3,6,12,24,48,...}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=6$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

$$
\frac{2}{3}\cdot {3}^{n}
$$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,3,\,6,\,12,\,24,\,48,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =2 \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =\frac{12}{6} \\  & =\frac{24}{12} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=6,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =6\cdot {2}^{n-1} \\  & =6\cdot {2}^{n}\cdot {2}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{6}{2}\cdot {2}^{n} \\  & =3\cdot {2}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={3\cdot {2}^{n}\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
Describe the set $S={…,\frac{1}{4},1,4,16,64,...}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=4$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

$$
{4}^{n}
$$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,\frac{1}{4},\,1,\,4,\,16,\,64,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =4 \\  & =\frac{(1)}{(\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =\frac{4}{1} \\  & =\frac{16}{4} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=4,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =4\cdot {4}^{n-1} \\  & =4\cdot {4}^{n}\cdot {4}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{4}{4}\cdot {4}^{n} \\  & ={4}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={{4}^{n}\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

content.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,\frac{1}{4},\,1,\,4,\,16,\,64,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =4 \\  & =\frac{(1)}{(\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =\frac{4}{1} \\  & =\frac{16}{4} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=4,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =4\cdot {4}^{n-1} \\  & =4\cdot {4}^{n}\cdot {4}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{4}{4}\cdot {4}^{n} \\  & ={4}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={{4}^{n}\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Describe the set $S={1,2,3,…,29}$ using a conditional definition.

$$
N
$$
after.worked_solution:
The set $S$ contains all natural numbers less than or equal to $29.$

In other words, $S$ contains all natural numbers less than $30,$ *excluding* $30.$

Therefore, the set can be written as 

$$
S={x\in N\,:\,x<30}.
$$

**Note**: This definition is not unique. For example:

- We can write $x\in Z.$ This gives

$$
S={x\in Z\,:\,0<x<30}.
$$

- We can write $x\le 29.$ This gives

$$
S={x\in N\,:\,x\le 29},
$$

or, writing $x\in Z$ as before, we have

$$
S={x\in Z\,:1\le x\le 29}.
$$

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
Describe the set $S={-6,-5,-4,...,12}$ using a conditional definition.

$$
R
$$
after.worked_solution:
The set $S$ contains all integer numbers between $-6$ and $12$ (including $-6$ and $12$).

Therefore, the set can be written as

$$
S={x\in Z\,:\,-6\le x\le 12}.
$$

**Note**: This definition is not unique. For example:

- We can write $-7<x<13.$ This gives

$$
S={x\in Z\,:\,-7<x<13}.
$$

content.worked_solution:
The set $S$ contains all integer numbers between $-6$ and $12$ (including $-6$ and $12$).

Therefore, the set can be written as

$$
S={x\in Z\,:\,-6\le x\le 12}.
$$

**Note**: This definition is not unique. For example:

$$
S={x\in Z\,:\,-7<x<13}.
$$

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
Describe the set $S={1,2,3,4,…,10}$ using a conditional definition.

$$
N
$$
after.worked_solution:
The set $S$ contains all natural numbers less than or equal to $10.$

Therefore, the set can be written as

$$
S={x\in N\,:\,x\le 10}.
$$

**Note**: This definition is not unique. For example:

- We can write $x\in Z.$ This gives

$$
S={x\in Z\,:1\le x\le 10}.
$$

- We can write $x<11.$ This gives

$$
S={x\in N\,:\,x<11},
$$

or, writing $x\in Z$ as before, we have

$$
S={x\in Z\,:\,0<x<11}.
$$

Question 13

Describe the set S={1,2,3,4,…,10} using a conditional definition.

N
Q
C
N
R
10
9
10
11
S={x∈{(Q)(S0)}:x≤{(9)(S1)}}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The set S contains all natural numbers less than or equal to 10.

Therefore, the set can be written as

S={x∈N:x≤10}.

Note: This definition is not unique. For example:

  • We can write x∈Z. This gives S={x∈Z:1≤x≤10}.

  • We can write x<11. This gives S={x∈N:x<11}, or, writing x∈Z as before, we have S={x∈Z:0<x<11}.

content.knowledge_point: Expressing a Set Using a Conditional Definition
content.problem:
Describe the set $S={1,2,3,4,…,10}$ using a conditional definition.

$$
Q
$$
content.worked_solution:
The set $S$ contains all natural numbers less than or equal to $10.$

Therefore, the set can be written as

$$
S={x\in N\,:\,x\le 10}.
$$

**Note**: This definition is not unique. For example:

- We can write $x\in Z.$ This gives

$$
S={x\in Z\,:1\le x\le 10}.
$$

- We can write $x<11.$ This gives

$$
S={x\in N\,:\,x<11},
$$

or, writing $x\in Z$ as before, we have

$$
S={x\in Z\,:\,0<x<11}.
$$

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
Describe the set $S={5,6,7,…}$ using a conditional definition.

$$
N
$$
after.worked_solution:
The set $S$ contains all natural numbers greater than or equal to $5.$

Therefore, the set can be written as

$$
S={x\in N\,:\,x\ge 5}.
$$

**Note**: This definition is not unique. For example:

- We can write $x\in Z.$ This gives

$$
S={x\in Z\,:x\ge 5}.
$$

- We can write $x>4.$ This gives

$$
S={x\in N\,:\,x>4},
$$

or, writing $x\in Z$ as before, we have

$$
S={x\in Z\,:\,x>4}.
$$
